deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is section 1 of Riemann's 'Mechanik des Ohres', a passage on method, and it continues the previous page. Its argument runs as follows.

(a) The first way starts from the structure of the organ and reasons from causes to effects. The anatomist takes it most naturally: studying each component, he asks what influence that part may have on the organ's function.

(b) In the physiology of the organs of motion this method works. It would work equally well for the sense organs if the physical properties of the individual parts could be determined.

(c) For microscopic objects, however, determining these properties from observation is always more or less uncertain and in any case highly imprecise.

(d) One is therefore forced to fill the gaps by analogy or teleology, which brings in the greatest arbitrariness.

(e) Conclusion: for the sense organs the synthetic procedure seldom gives correct results and never gives certain ones.

The page heading 'Synthetischer Weg' follows the Newtonian usage, in which synthesis runs from causes to effects. That sets up the next page, 'Analytischer Weg', which runs from the given functions to their causes. That method has three steps: find a sufficient hypothesis, examine how far it is necessary, and compare it with experience. It is the method Riemann then applies to the mechanics of the middle ear.

The page itself is a clean copy in a calligraphic hand, not Riemann's autograph. This fits the previous page's header 'Aus dem Nachlass von B. Riemann', and suggests it is a fair copy prepared for the posthumous edition, probably via Henle. Nothing on the page needs to be filled in mathematically.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible on this page because there is no mathematics on it.

There is a terminological inconsistency with the previous page as transcribed. There the 'first way' (from structure, causes to effects) is called analytic and the second synthetic. This page heads its discussion of the first way 'Synthetischer Weg', and the next page heads the second way 'Analytischer Weg'. The Newtonian usage (analysis = from effects to causes, synthesis = from causes to effects) agrees with this page's headings. Either the previous page's transcription swaps the two words, or the copyist or the manuscript does. If I recall the published 1867 text correctly, it reads 'den ersten Weg den synthetischen, den zweiten den analytischen' (unsure). The previous page should be rechecked against its image.

results.what: Methodological critique of the 'synthetic' (structure-to-function) approach in sense-organ physiology. Its two weaknesses are that the physical properties of microscopic parts cannot be measured precisely, and that the gaps then have to be filled by analogy or teleology.
results.modern_name: Bottom-up/forward modelling versus inverse (function-to-mechanism) modelling. This is an early statement of the ill-determined-parameters problem in biomechanics.
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, 'Mechanik des Ohres', published posthumously by J. Henle (Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, 1867) and in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke. The analysis/synthesis terminology goes back to Newton and Herbart.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a non-mathematical passage on method from Riemann's well-known posthumous paper on the mechanics of the ear. It is published and was already attributed to him in 1867.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well. 'veranlasst' is written with ß in the image ('veranlaßt').
The '2' at the top left is a page or section number in the margin, not part of the text.
Spelling as in the image: 'Thätigkeit', 'Bestandtheile', 'genöthigt', 'Willkür', 'ließen' are correctly rendered.
The hand is a clean calligraphic copy rather than Riemann's own autograph. This is worth noting in the metadata.
